sep5.caption:
Most gifts for kids come in wrapping paper. For the children in this project, one of the most important gifts is an ID card.

Their story is at https://directory.rawcs.com.au/26-2014-15, and it starts with a long walk. Many of them travelled for days into Thailand, alone or with their siblings, to escape the war in Myanmar. Without Thai identification they can't go to school, see a doctor properly or travel freely, so getting that sorted is often the first real step toward a normal life.

Borderless Friendship, run through the Rotary Club of Melville, helps with that, along with hostel accommodation and schooling. $3,000 covers a weekend workshop for 50 teenagers on health and relationships education.

There's a short video on the project page if you'd like to meet the community. This season of giving, you can help a child feel safe, schooled and at home.

sep15.caption:
Only about 1 in 100 rural girls in the part of Tanzania where Orkeeswa Secondary School operates make it as far as Year 11 or 12, in a region where most families live on less than $1.25 a day. Students at Orkeeswa are beating those odds, topping national exams, and a good number return afterwards to teach in their own community.

The newest classroom needs an outdoor learning space, some AV equipment and two whiteboards. $12.50 covers a whiteboard, $50 covers a piece of AV equipment, and $125 covers a section of the outdoor space.

There's a short video of the school and its students on the project page if you'd like to see it.

When the Trishuli corridor was buried on 26 August 2026, taking hundreds of lives and leaving more than 10,000 households without shelter, Nepali Rotarians turned to their neighbours and Australian Rotarians turned to their phones. Same handshake, same promise, two hemispheres.

They cover what Rotarians on the ground are seeing and how clubs in Nepal and Australia are working together. 

Rotary District 3292 is mobilising volunteers for relief distribution, while RAWCS has opened the Nepal Flooding Disaster Relief Fund, channelling donations through Rotary contacts in Nepal for shelter, cash grants and clean water.

Every club can play a part.

More than two weeks after Nepal's Trishuli corridor was buried, the need has not eased. It has simply moved out of the headlines.

Over 10,000 households remain without shelter following the flooding on 26 August 2026. Rotarians in Nepal are still working through the same channels that make disaster response effective: local contacts, quick decisions and funds that reach families directly, without delay or red tape.

sep2.caption:
For more than twenty years, the Tender Foot Self Help School has been part of daily life in Nairobi's Kangemi slum, offering food, clothing and a nursery-to-Grade-8 education to children who would otherwise go without. It has run continuously since 2003.

That kind of consistency depends on the Rotary Club of Emerald & District, and on the people who give to this project year after year.

You can support this project here: https://directory.rawcs.com.au/ProjectDisplayBB.aspx?1-2003-04

sep3.caption:
The Lighthart Project looks after forty children and young people with cognitive or multiple disabilities in Stung Mean Chey, on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, many of whom would otherwise be left out of school altogether.

Some sensory equipment donated from Australia has recently reached the classroom. Beyond that, what the project needs is fairly ordinary: books, desks, teacher salaries, and rent to keep the classroom itself open.

You can find out more and support this project here: https://directory.rawcs.com.au/ProjectDisplayBB.aspx?140-2010-11

sep4.caption:
In Goma, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, a group of mothers called Mama Wimbi sew backpacks, uniforms and school supplies for children who have fled violence and arrived with nothing.

A SchoolKit means one less thing for a family to worry about when they're already stretched between food, housing and school fees. A spare uniform matters too, since clean water is scarce and one uniform can't always be washed often enough to avoid scabies outbreaks in crowded classrooms.

Because the kits are made locally rather than shipped in, a donation also supports the women doing the sewing, and helps them provide for their own children.

There's a short video on the project page showing how the kits are made. You can read more and support the project here: https://directory.rawcs.com.au/ProjectDisplayBB.aspx?23-2023-24

oct-butterfly-buddies.caption:
As Breast Cancer Awareness Month draws to a close, let’s keep the conversation going.

A simple chat with a friend or loved one can be the nudge they need to book a screening.

At this year’s Rotary Pioneer Adventure Day, BreastScreen SA’s mobile clinic screened 47 women on site. 44 received the all-clear, and three are now having follow-up tests. It’s a powerful reminder of why accessible screening and early detection matter.

Beyond Australia, Butterfly Buddies, supported by the Rotary Club of North Lake Macquarie, helps women in Fiji and across the South Pacific after a mastectomy. The project provides repurposed breast forms and mastectomy bras, and trains local nurses and community workers to fit them so women can regain comfort and confidence.

Make a donation today to help Butterfly Buddies reach more women.

Waste that ends up on the foreshores of Central Coast waterways, especially in the mangroves, doesn't clear itself.
